structure.title: CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY
structure.heading: 5 CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY
structure.start_phrase: Information pursuant to the sustainability statement is presented in Chapter 5 of this Universal Registration Document in parts 5.1 to 5.6 as well as in Chapter 3 for corporate governance information, Chapter 4 for the risk management framework, cybersecurity and compliance risks and Chapter 10 for detailed tables relating to the European Taxonomy.
structure.summary:
- Context and scope: Extract from Societe Generale’s Universal Registration Document 2025, Chapter 5 on Corporate Social Responsibility, presenting the Group’s first CSRD-compliant sustainability statement (per ESRS), subject to limited assurance by external auditors and approved by the Board on March 6, 2025. It references related content in other chapters (corporate governance, risk and cybersecurity, and detailed EU Taxonomy tables).
- Regulatory background and assurance: Explains the CSRD objective to harmonize ESG reporting, the ESRS coverage across environmental, social, and business conduct topics, and the use of French H2A guidance for the new assurance mission.
- CSR strategy and governance: Reaffirms the Group’s purpose and four CSR pillars—environmental transition, positive local impact, responsible employer, and culture of responsibility—overseen by the Executive Committee and Board, with support from a non-voting director expert in environmental transition.
- Double materiality approach: States that only material information is disclosed; materiality is determined via a double materiality assessment (impact and financial) grounded in the Group’s risk management and internal control framework, with plans to enhance methodologies as partner data availability improves.
- Structure of the sustainability statement:
  - 5.1 General information: principles, sustainability strategy, impacts/risks/opportunities (IROs), and governance of sustainability issues.
  - 5.2 Environmental information under the EU Taxonomy: eligible and aligned activities.
  - 5.3 Climate change: material climate IROs, transition plan, mitigation management, Group-attributed GHG emissions, climate risk management, and climate-related opportunities.
  - 5.4 Social information: own workforce; consumers and end users.
  - 5.5 Business conduct: management of material impacts and risks, and cybersecurity.
  - 5.6 Lookup tables: links to data points required by other EU legislation and to material disclosure requirements.
  - 5.7 Report on certification of sustainability information and Article 8 EU Taxonomy disclosures.
  - 5.8 Duty of Care Plan: introduction; mapping and assessment of inherent environmental and social risks; prevention and mitigation actions; whistleblowing procedures; monitoring and reporting on effectiveness; outlook and planned developments.

nodes.title: GENERAL INFORMATION
nodes.heading: 5.1 GENERAL INFORMATION
nodes.start_phrase:
Societe Generale has prepared its consolidated sustainability 
statement for the year ended 31 December 2024, in accordance with:
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Introduction to Societe Generale’s consolidated sustainability statement for the year ended 31 December 2024, within the 2025 Universal Registration Document (CSR section).
- Reporting framework: Prepared in accordance with the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD; French Order 2023‑1142) and the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS; Commission Delegated Regulation 2023/2772). Overlaps with other French/EU regulations will be flagged in relevant sections.
- First-time application: Acknowledges interpretation uncertainties and an initial double materiality analysis without established market practices or comparatives. Emphasizes verifiability and understandability based on information available at Executive Board approval.
- Use of estimates and limitations: Disclosures may rely on estimates subject to refinement. Current limitations affect:
  - Activities included in the materiality assessment (IROs)
  - EU Taxonomy eligibility/alignment determinations
  - Scope of the Climate Change Mitigation Transition Plan
  - Selection of underlying assets for attributed (financed) GHG emissions calculations
  - Inclusion of entities with more than 10 employees for own-operations reporting
- Continuous improvement: The Group may adapt content, data collection, disclosure processes, and internal controls as CSRD/ESRS evolve, additional guidance and best practices emerge, and data availability improves.
- Perimeter of reporting: Group-level consolidation covering the parent company, controlled entities (including those issuing their own sustainability statements), and holdings in joint ventures and associates, across value chains identified as material. Results of the IROs assessment are referenced in section 5.1.3.1.
- Subsidiaries with standalone sustainability statements: Ayvens SAS (France), BRD – Groupe Societe Generale SA (Romania), and Komerční Banka AS (Czech Republic).

nodes.title: General principles relating to the sustainability statement
nodes.heading: 5.1.1 General principles relating to the sustainability statement
nodes.start_phrase: Societe Generale has prepared its consolidated sustainability statement for the year ended 31 December 2024, in accordance with:
nodes.summary:
- Context and scope: Extract from Societe Generale’s Universal Registration Document 2025, Corporate Social Responsibility section, presenting the Group’s consolidated sustainability statement for FY2024 at Group level (parent, controlled entities, JVs and associates) and across material parts of the value chain.

- Reporting framework: Prepared in accordance with the CSRD (French Order No. 2023-1142) and ESRS (EU Delegated Regulation 2023/2772). Acknowledges overlaps with other French/EU regulations, referenced where relevant.

- First-time application: Notes interpretation uncertainties and an initial double materiality assessment without established benchmarks. Focuses on ESRS compliance using available data, resulting in:
  - Use of estimates and proxies, with methodologies/assumptions to be refined.
  - Perimeter limitations for: materiality assessment coverage; EU Taxonomy eligibility/alignment; Climate Change Mitigation Transition Plan scope; selection of underlying assets for financed GHG emissions; and reporting on entities with >10 employees for own operations.
  - Commitment to continuous improvement as standards, guidance, interpretations, and external data mature.

- Perimeter and subsidiaries:
  - Subsidiaries publishing their own statements: Ayvens SAS (France), BRD – Groupe Societe Generale SA (Romania), Komerční Banka AS (Czech Republic).
  - Subsidiaries exempt from publishing their own statements (using consolidation exemption but referencing the Group’s statement): Boursorama SA, Compagnie générale de location d’équipements SA, Fiditalia SPA, Franfinance SA, GEFA Bank GmbH, Société Générale Luxembourg SA, Sogecap SA.

- Disclosure exemptions: Uses French Commercial Code options (L.232-6-3 and L.233-28-4) to omit impending developments or matters under negotiation.

- Time horizons: Short term (≤1 year), medium term (1–5 years), long term (>5 years), with deviations disclosed where applicable.

- Estimates and uncertainties:
  - Many metrics—especially value-chain and financed GHG emissions—rely on estimates, averages, multiple external data sources, and emission factors that vary by source/context.
  - Highlights data quality limits, methodological diversity, and evolving regulation; provides metric-specific explanations where needed.
  - Forward-looking statements reflect ambitions, are subject to significant risks/uncertainties, and depend on local legal constraints; they are trajectories, not guarantees.

- Content and presentation changes:
  - Transition from NFRD/DPEF (since 2017) to CSRD/ESRS with tighter requirements and a four-part structure: general, environmental, social, governance.
  - Sector-specific ESRS for financial institutions expected from FY2026 at the earliest.
  - Allows inclusion of additional material, Group-specific topics.
  - Incorporation by reference to other chapters for certain ESRS disclosures (e.g., governance GOV-1 to GOV-3, cybersecurity) and to IFRS notes where ESRS topics have material financial impacts.

- Sustainability strategy:
  - Clarifies definitions: CSR (covering ESG), ESRS sustainability matters (environmental: climate, pollution, water, biodiversity, resources/circular economy; social: own workforce, value chain workers, communities, consumers/end-users; governance: business conduct), sustainable finance, and stakeholders.
  - Key figures: 2024 net banking income EUR 26.8bn; ~119,000 employees in 60+ countries with regional distribution.
  - CSR ambition built on four pillars: environmental transition, positive local impact, responsible employer, culture of responsibility.
  - Accelerated ESG ambitions include: reducing fossil fuel exposures and aligning portfolios with the Paris Agreement; dedicating EUR 1bn to transition investments; contributing ~EUR 500bn to sustainable finance; an envelope of EUR 100bn to reduce gender pay gap; and expanding partnerships and participation in international initiatives.

- Cross-references noted to sections on materiality outcomes (IROs and links to strategy/business model), EU Taxonomy, climate transition plan, and financed emissions scope.

nodes.title: Sustainability strategy
nodes.heading: 5.1.2 Sustainability strategy
nodes.start_phrase: “Corporate Social Responsibility” (CSR) covers all sustainability and sustainable development matters, including environmental, social and governance (ESG) matters.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and framing: Defines Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) as encompassing all ESG and sustainability matters, aligned with ESRS topical standards. Clarifies key terms (sustainable finance, stakeholders, business model, value chain, business segments).
- Group profile and key figures: 2024 net banking income of EUR 26.8 billion; ~119,000 employees across 60+ countries with geographic breakdown. Diverse customer base spanning individuals to sovereigns, and activities in retail banking, corporate and investment banking, private banking, insurance, and specialized services.
- Strategy and CSR ambition: Purpose is “Building together… a better and sustainable future.” Strategic plan to 2026 accelerates ESG: reduce fossil fuel exposures and align portfolios with the Paris Agreement; increase transition finance (EUR 1 billion envelope); contribute ~EUR 500 billion in sustainable finance; EUR 100 billion envelope to reduce gender pay gap; expand partnerships and international initiatives. Four CSR pillars: environmental transition, positive local impact, responsible employer, and culture of responsibility.
- Business lines and organization: Three complementary pillars with NBI split—French Retail, Private Banking and Insurance; Global Banking and Investor Services; Mobility, International Retail Banking and Financial Services (32%/37%/31% of NBI).
- Business models and value chains: Two distinct business models—(1) core banking and insurance; (2) specialized mobility (Ayvens) and real estate development (Sogeprom)—with differing revenue profiles, services, and customers. Value chain described across upstream (procurement), own operations (HR, real estate, IT, liquidity/risk management, compliance), and downstream (products/services to customers).
- Upstream and own operations: EUR 5.5 billion external expenditure focused on IT, software, audit, and consulting; supplier relationships spanning large corporates, SMEs, and start-ups. Own operations emphasize HR management, property management, and critical IT for continuity and security.
- Downstream offerings: Comprehensive financing and advisory for corporates/SMEs (structured finance, M&A, project finance, syndicated loans, payments); retail banking and private banking (deposits, loans, payments, wealth management); investment banking (markets, advisory, IPOs, debt issuance); integrated insurance (life, non-life, protection); asset management and securities services; specialized mobility solutions (leasing, fleet, multimodality) and real estate development.
- Value creation narrative: Corporate purpose and values (Team Spirit, Innovation, Responsibility, Commitment) linked to client outcomes—supporting projects, ecological transition, innovative services, protection, responsible savings, and secure transactions.
- Role in value chains: Ethical management of procurement and operations (Purchasing and HR roles, SSE focus, climate impact reduction). Customer value via embedded ESG products, transition financing, ESG advisory, insurance and securities services with ESG indicators, and sustainable mobility solutions. Contribution to communities and SDG-aligned infrastructure financing.
- Stakeholder engagement: Structured dialogue with five families—civil society (regulators, NGOs, media), investment community (shareholders, investors, rating agencies), customers, employees (including unions, students), and partners (suppliers, industry associations). Describes channels (meetings, consultations, surveys, NPS, events, whistleblowing, complaint mechanisms), 2024 topics (regulation, climate strategy, HR/D&I, performance, risks, AI/innovation, customer experience), and how feedback informs strategy, policies, offerings, and purchasing.
- Impacts, Risks and Opportunities (IROs) and double materiality: Explains the ESRS-based double materiality approach across the whole value chain. Material IROs concentrate on: financing and life insurance (downstream), specialized services (mobility) across the chain, and own operations (workforce and business conduct). Notes additional material themes not covered by ESRS—cybersecurity and employee engagement—addressed in dedicated sections.

nodes.title: Impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs)
nodes.heading: 5.1.3 Impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs)
nodes.start_phrase: The concept of IRO covers impacts, risks and opportunities related to environmental, social and governance (ESG) topics.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Defines the ESG Impacts, Risks and Opportunities (IROs) framework underpinning Societe Generale’s sustainability statement, built on double materiality across the value chain (upstream, own operations, downstream). Subsidiaries with separate sustainability statements disclose their own IROs.

- Material topics identified:
  - Climate change (E1) across banking, insurance, and specialized services.
  - Own workforce (S1) focusing on working conditions, equal treatment, engagement.
  - Consumers and end‑users (S4) covering privacy/data protection and fair marketing/access.
  - Business conduct (G1) including supplier relations, culture, whistleblowing, anti‑corruption, cybersecurity.
  - Cybersecurity and employee engagement are treated as material by the Group though not covered by ESRS topical standards.

- Banking and insurance IROs (with value‑chain level and horizons):
  - Impacts: financed emissions (corporate financing) and emissions linked to life insurance investments are material and negative (downstream; short/medium/long term).
  - Risks: climate transition and physical risks heighten credit, counterparty and business risks across activities and time horizons; potential collateral value declines.
  - Opportunities: short‑/medium‑term revenue from supporting client low‑carbon transition in corporate, CIB, retail and trade finance.
  - S1 impacts: potential negative effects on employees (working conditions/equal treatment) and positive societal impact via employee engagement and philanthropy.
  - S4 impacts/risks: risks to customer privacy/data and fair marketing/access; counterparties’ consumer‑related compliance failures can translate into credit risk.
  - G1 impacts/risks: risks tied to supplier payment practices, culture, whistleblowing, anti‑corruption, cybersecurity; counterparties’ weak governance can create credit risk.

- Specialized services (Ayvens mobility/leasing) IROs:
  - E1: material emissions from vehicle manufacture, use, and after resale.
  - E2: pollution across lifecycle stages.
  - E5: resource use in manufacture/maintenance.
  - S2: occupational health and safety in supply chain; mixed employment effects from electrification.
  - Ayvens sets its own policies/actions/targets; its GHGs are consolidated in Group inventory.

- Strategy integration and business model:
  - Decarbonization of high‑emission sector financing, client transition support, and partnerships in environmental solutions.
  - Responsible employer strategy with quantified goals on QoL at work, equity, inclusion, development to drive engagement/performance.
  - Customer focus via NPS and service improvements.
  - Ethical culture and business conduct as core commitments.

- Financial materiality, effects and mitigation:
  - No material adjustments to asset/liability carrying amounts required as of 31 Dec 2024.
  - Credit, counterparty and business risks from climate captured in budgeting (climate‑stressed trajectory) and ICAAP add‑ons; mitigations include ESG‑embedded lending policies, exclusions, NZBA targets, margining, sectoral steering.
  - Opportunities quantified via projected sustainable finance revenues in short/medium term.

- Resilience analysis:
  - ECB‑aligned identification/assessment of climate & environmental risks by BU, region, sector, product.
  - Annual double materiality and Business Environment Scan (BES) inform strategy and budgets.
  - Use of three core climate scenarios (Below 2°C, Net Zero 2050, Current Policies) across short/medium/long horizons; governance bodies oversee process.

- Methodologies to identify and assess IROs:
  - Transmission channels: microeconomic (direct) and macroeconomic (indirect) pathways from ESG factors to financial effects.
  - Impact materiality four‑step process: mapping and transmission channels; internal quantitative/qualitative assessment; stakeholder input; consolidation. Severity (scale, scope, irremediability) and likelihood scored; focus primarily on negative impacts given evidentiary standards for positives; data gaps acknowledged, especially downstream.
  - Financial materiality: identify key risks/opportunities, quantify potential effects by horizon/frequency, compare to Group materiality thresholds (Risk Appetite Framework). ESG risks treated as factors intensifying traditional risk categories. Continuous and annual risk identification; criteria include materiality vs thresholds and scenario frequency.
  - Tools: climate stress tests; internal vulnerability indicators (ICVI, CCVI, SCVI) and nature risk indicator (INVI).

- Topical applications:
  - Climate impacts: quantified using Group GHG data and PCAF for financed emissions; insurance assessed via emissions of corporate equities/bonds.
  - Climate risks: quantified under internal scenarios (Net Zero 2050, Below 2°C, Current Policies) with sector/region lenses; stress tests inform management.
  - Climate opportunities: material for corporate and trade finance; others considered even if not yet quantified.
  - Nature (pollution, water, biodiversity, resources/circularity): mixed quantitative (e.g., ENCORE) and qualitative methods; credit/counterparty risks estimated using internal nature vulnerability; methodology under enhancement due to data/method limits.
  - Business conduct: qualitative assessment per ESRS sub‑topics; governance weaknesses at counterparties can trigger operational, reputational and credit impacts.

- ESRS disclosures:
  - Cross‑reference tables indicate where ESRS‑referenced datapoints and topical materiality conclusions are disclosed.

- Governance of sustainability:
  - Governance bodies include Board of Directors (and committees) and General Management (CEO and Deputy CEO).
  - Board sets strategic guidelines, approves CSR strategy, sustainability statement, climate transition plan, and double materiality outcomes; supported by a non‑voting Director dedicated to CSR.
  - Committees:
    - Audit and Internal Control: reviews sustainability disclosures and internal control framework; reports to Board.
    - Risk: reviews sustainability‑related risks, climate stress tests, and risk materiality; supports ESG risk appetite.
    - Compensation: advises on CSR criteria in executive remuneration.
    - Nomination and Corporate Governance: ensures Board has requisite CSR skills and governance arrangements.

nodes.title: Governance of sustainability issues
nodes.heading: 5.1.4 Governance of sustainability issues
nodes.start_phrase: The following sections describe the governance processes, controls and procedures in place to control, manage and monitor sustainability matters.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and structure: Outlines Societe Generale’s governance, controls, and procedures for managing sustainability matters, with cross-references to Corporate Governance for detailed composition and rules.

- Governance bodies and roles:
  - Board of Directors: Sets business guidelines integrating CSR, approves the CSR strategy and sustainability statement (including the climate transition plan and double materiality outcomes), and oversees procedures and controls for material sustainability issues. Supported by a non-voting Director dedicated to CSR who contributes to strategy preparation and attends relevant committee meetings.
  - Specialized Board committees:
    - Audit and Internal Control Committee: Oversees processes and internal controls for sustainability information; reviews financial and extra-financial CSR disclosures prior to Board approval.
    - Risk Committee: Reviews ESG and climate risks, climate stress tests, and the risk materiality assessment; informs ESG-related risk appetite.
    - Compensation Committee: Recommends CSR-linked criteria in executive remuneration.
    - Nomination and Corporate Governance Committee: Ensures governance fitness for CSR, maintains a Board skills matrix on CSR topics, and guides director recruitment and training.
  - General Management: Proposes the CSR strategy (notably on climate) with action plans and timelines; reports annually on progress. The Deputy CEO oversees CSR policy integration across Business and Service Units.

- Group-level committees chaired by the Deputy CEO:
  - Responsible Commitments Committee: Decision-making body for E&S responsibility; sets Group E&S commitments and standards (e.g., sectoral policies, portfolio alignment), and reviews products/businesses with E&S risk.
  - Group Risk Committee: Validates risk taxonomy, identification, stress testing, Risk Inventory, and Risk Appetite Framework; embeds ESG in sectoral risk committees; annually reviews environmental topics and ESG risk governance.
  - Complex Transactions and Reputational Risk Committee: Reviews complex transactions and activities with elevated legal/regulatory/compliance/accounting/conduct/reputational risks.
  - Client Acceptance Committee: Decides on client onboarding/continuation based on non-compliance and reputational risks (including CSR) and exceptions to CSR standards.

- Expertise and training: Directors possess and annually reassess adequate CSR expertise; the Board’s training program includes CSR. In 2024, training covered CSRD, double materiality, governance responsibilities, and outcomes; similar briefings were provided to General Management and the Executive Committee.

- Decision-making and reporting:
  - IROs and sustainability statement follow the financial statements’ governance path: the Finance Division presents drafts to the Audit and Internal Control Committee; the Board approves, informed by the non-voting Director.
  - Double materiality analysis involved business, Finance, Risk, and CSR; validated by the Executive Committee and shapes disclosure content and strategy.
  - Board materials generally include relevant social and environmental considerations.
  - Executive compensation integrates CSR performance targets aligned with Group CSR strategy.

- Due diligence framework: Summarizes core elements—embedding in governance/strategy/business model, stakeholder engagement, identifying/assessing negative impacts, taking action, and tracking/communicating effectiveness—referencing detailed sections.

- ESG risk management and internal controls over sustainability reporting:
  - ESG risks are treated as aggravating factors within existing risk categories, integrated into standard processes (identification, quantification, appetite, monitoring, reporting, control, mitigation) in line with EBA guidance.
  - Outputs inform the Risk Appetite Framework/Statement, stress testing (including climate), and ICAAP; results feed business strategic reviews via the risk inventory.
  - Regular reporting cadence to General Management and the Board’s Risk Committee includes dashboards of ESG risk appetite indicators and topical analyses.
  - Control framework: Quality/relevance checks and a double-validation mechanism support the double materiality assessment and sustainability statement production; Level 1 and Level 2 controls are coordinated by the Finance Division, with enhancements planned in 2025 through tool-integrated internal controls.
  - Roles of expert functions: Sustainability Department develops ESG normative documentation and E&S impact management systems; Finance Division produces ESG indicators, manages regulatory monitoring, and compiles the sustainability statement.

- European Taxonomy disclosures:
  - Presents taxonomy-eligible and aligned activities and climate-related information, including the Green Asset Ratio (GAR).
  - Explains structural limitations of GAR for diversified, international banks and exclusions (e.g., SMEs and non-EU exposures) that depress alignment ratios and underrepresent transition support.
  - Notes that while Taxonomy KPIs inform strategic thinking, current design and data gaps limit their representativeness; relevance is expected to improve as methodologies and data evolve.

nodes.title: ENVIRONMENTAL INFORMATION RELATED TO ELIGIBLE AND ALIGNED ACTIVITIES UNDER THE EUROPEAN TAXONOMY
nodes.heading: 5.2 ENVIRONMENTAL INFORMATION RELATED TO ELIGIBLE AND ALIGNED ACTIVITIES UNDER THE EUROPEAN TAXONOMY
nodes.start_phrase:
The environmental information in this Sustainability Statement includes 
the information on the activities eligible and aligned with the European 
Taxonomy presented in this section as well as the information related to 
climate change presented in the next section (5.3).
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Societe Generale’s 2025 Universal Registration Document presents environmental disclosures under the EU Taxonomy (EU 2020/852), incorporating Delegated Regulations 2021/2178 and 2023/2486 and related FAQs, with KPIs required from 1 January 2024. It links Taxonomy reporting (section 5.2) with climate change disclosures (section 5.3).

- Green Asset Ratio (GAR) definition and structural limits: GAR measures the share of Taxonomy‑aligned exposures over covered assets. It is structurally low for diversified EU banks, especially with significant non‑EU, CIB, and SME activities. Current methodology excludes many exposures (notably SMEs and non‑EU undertakings not subject to NFRD/CSRD) from eligibility/alignment and does not capture transition‑supporting activities, creating a gap between GAR and the bank’s broader sustainable finance efforts. Data availability and quality constrain KPIs but are expected to improve.

- GAR and KPI results (high level):
  - Balance sheet overview: Total assets ~EUR 1,417 bn; covered assets ~EUR 713 bn (excludes trading book, sovereigns/central banks/supranationals, certain interbank and non‑transactional assets).
  - Eligibility/alignment concentration: Eligibility largely from retail mortgage loans and exposures to EU NFRD entities; activities with SMEs, non‑EU companies, and many renewable project financings of non‑NFRD entities are not eligible.
  - Alignment ratios (stock): Turnover alignment ~1.71%; CapEx alignment ~1.88%. Aligned assets c. EUR 12.2 bn. Coverage is roughly half of total assets, with substantial exclusions from both numerator and denominator under Article 8 rules.
  - Asset class highlights: Households/retail drive eligibility (c. EUR 129.7 bn eligible; c. EUR 10.4 bn aligned). Non‑financial corporates show smaller eligible/aligned amounts; financial corporates contribute marginally.
  - Additional KPIs: GAR flow aligned assets c. EUR 1.7 bn with low alignment ratios (~1%). Financial guarantees show environmentally sustainable amounts (c. EUR 7.4 bn). Assets under management include a smaller aligned share (c. EUR 0.6 bn). Trading book and fees/commissions KPIs apply from 2026; SME inclusion remains subject to impact assessment.

- Methodology for EU Taxonomy implementation:
  - Alignment requires substantial contribution under Technical Screening Criteria, DNSH across five other environmental objectives, and Minimum Social Safeguards; many eligible activities do not align due to stringent, granular criteria and data gaps.
  - Data sources and governance rely on EBA Pillar 3 recommendations and EC FAQs. Certain subsidiary indicators (e.g., Societe Generale Assurances) will be disclosed separately; other exempt entities and the financial conglomerate indicator may be published later.
  - Additional required disclosures include Taxonomy‑aligned shares in Financial Guarantees and Assets under Management at end‑2024.

- Alignment calculation approaches:
  - Corporates and public sector (non‑retail): Alignment counted only where counterparties subject to NFRD/CSRD publish Turnover/CapEx KPIs and related evidence. Dedicated use‑of‑proceeds loans to NFRD entities are generally eligible but often unaligned absent client data. General‑purpose lending uses published counterparty KPIs. Exposures to local housing offices (OPH) are eligible but not aligned due to data unavailability.
  - Retail (households): Mortgages are eligible; alignment requires EPC A or top‑15% primary energy performance (e.g., for pre‑2021 buildings) plus DNSH (including physical risk screening) and MSS. Data for alignment is scarce, so only a small share aligns. Guaranteed mortgages (e.g., Crédit Logement) are eligible; alignment follows TSC/DNSH. Portfolio assessed using national data (France) and RE2020 for new builds. Home renovation loans and consumer car loans are eligible; alignment has been assessed mainly for vehicle finance leases in Ayvens and CGI using Ayvens’ methodology.

- Decision logic: A process flow distinguishes covered vs excluded assets, NFRD eligibility, dedicated vs general‑purpose lending, and then tests TSC and DNSH (including physical risk) to determine eligibility and alignment across retail and non‑retail exposures.

- Fossil gas and nuclear disclosures: In line with Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1214, the Group discloses exposures to transitional activities in gas and nuclear. From 2024, nine templates per KPI category are required; Societe Generale publishes the most relevant set for GAR stock, with full templates available in the appendices.

- Climate change section (5.3) overview:
  - Strategy and resilience: The Group assesses climate resilience through its materiality analysis and Business Environment Scan, complemented by annual scenario‑based climate stress tests covering transition and physical risks across credit, counterparty, and business risks.
  - Scenarios and horizons: Uses “Current Policies,” “Below 2°C,” and “NZE 2050” scenarios over short (to 2026), medium (to 2030), and long‑term (to 2040/2050) horizons, with sectoral and geographic granularity and added shocks.
  - Use of results: Stress test outputs feed financial materiality assessments, Risk Appetite, Business Environment Scan, budgeting, and ICAAP.
  - Uncertainties: Long horizons, limited historical data, evolving methodologies, and challenges in linking climate factors to risk categories introduce material uncertainty in stress test outcomes.

nodes.title: ENVIRONMENTAL INFORMATION RELATED TO CLIMATE CHANGE
nodes.heading: 5.3 ENVIRONMENTAL INFORMATION RELATED TO CLIMATE CHANGE
nodes.start_phrase: The resilience of the Group’s strategy and business model is assured by both the materiality analysis and the Business Environment Scan (BES).
nodes.summary:
- Presents Societe Generale’s climate resilience analysis for its strategy and business model, built on the materiality assessment and the Business Environment Scan (BES).
- Details the integration (since 2022) of annual, scenario-based climate stress tests covering transition and physical risks, using three long-term scenarios (Current Policies, Below 2°C as reference, and NZE 2050), with sectoral/geographical granularity and shocks across short, medium, and long horizons.
- Defines scope and focus: financial materiality across all risk categories, with emphasis on credit risk (corporate and retail portfolios), counterparty risk (all derivatives and securities financing counterparties), and business risk (all Group activities). Counterparty risk analysis includes six market stress tests (NZE 2050 and Current Policies for 2025, 2030, 2040) and stressed default probabilities for climate-exposed sectors.
- Notes timing: stress tests and BES performed late 2023–early 2024; a new cycle started end-2024 with completion expected in Q2 2025.
- Explains how results inform the financial materiality assessment and feed into Risk Appetite, the BES, budgeting, and ICAAP, with outcomes linked to the description of climate-related material impacts, risks, and opportunities (IROs).
- Acknowledges key uncertainties in climate stress testing: long time horizons, limited historical data, variable data robustness, evolving/standardizing methodologies, and challenges in mapping climate risks to traditional risk categories.
- Adds that two additional stress tests address short- and medium-term shocks (2023–2026 and to 2030), modeling adverse slowdowns triggered by transition dynamics and climate hazards.

nodes.title: Climate change ‑related material IROs and their interaction with the strategy and business model
nodes.heading: 5.3.1 Climate change ‑related material IROs and their interaction with the strategy and business model
nodes.start_phrase: The resilience of the Group’s strategy and business model is assured by both the materiality analysis and the Business Environment Scan (BES).
nodes.summary:
- Focus area: Societe Generale’s climate-related disclosures within its CSR report, covering resilience of strategy and business model, material climate IROs (impacts, risks, opportunities), and an overview of the Group’s climate transition plan.
- Resilience approach: Combines double materiality assessment and Business Environment Scan (BES); main analytical tool is scenario-based climate stress testing integrated into Group stress tests since 2022.
- Stress test design: At least annual; global or portfolio scope; covers transition and physical risks across three long-term scenarios (Current Policies, Below 2°C, NZE 2050) with short-, medium-, and long-term shocks (including 2025, 2030, 2040; also 2040 and 2050 horizons).
- Risk coverage: Financial materiality assessed across all risk types, with emphasis on credit risk (corporate and retail), counterparty risk (all derivatives and SFT counterparties), and business risk (all activities).
- Methodology highlights: Use of ICVI transition and physical risk indicators for credit/counterparty risk; counterparty risk assessed via six market stress tests (NZE 2050 and Current Policies for 2025, 2030, 2040) and stressed PDs for exposed sectors.
- Use of results: Stress test outputs and expected financial effects inform financial materiality assessment, Risk Appetite, BES, annual budget, and ICAAP.
- Uncertainties: Long time horizons, limited historical data, evolving and non-standardized methodologies, and challenges linking climate drivers to risk categories.
- Material impacts: Mainly arise in downstream value chain through financing and investment activities.
- Credit risk (corporate): Transition risk driven by policy/regulation and technology (major, short-to-medium term), with behavioral shifts affecting medium/long term; physical risks increasingly material under slower transition (all physical hazards considered relevant long term and potentially earlier under adverse shocks). Sectors most exposed include Real Estate, Oil & Gas, Automotive, and Aviation.
- Credit risk (individual/professional customers): Vulnerabilities via income/profitability and collateral values; assessed as moderate and non-material across horizons under stated assumptions.
- Counterparty risk: Climate impacts PD via costs, revenues, assets; policy/regulation and technology relevant from short to long term; physical risks grow medium/long term. Exposure at default can shift via market valuations (notably carbon prices); mitigated in part by margining.
- Business risk: Measured as deviation from budget; budgets embed Below 2°C assumptions. Transition risks deemed material across all horizons; physical risks could be material long term in highly affected geographies. Key financial effects include policy/regulatory shocks and stakeholder behavior shifts affecting strategy, reputation, and resource allocation.
- Opportunities: Considered material, primarily in financing activities; detailed elsewhere in the report.
- Climate transition plan overview: Banks’ catalytic role in decarbonization; SG’s plan structured by high-emitting sectors and by activity (corporate financing and life insurance). Decarbonization levers are (1) aligning financing portfolios of most emission-intensive sectors with Paris Agreement pathways and (2) aligning life insurance asset portfolios likewise.
- Strategic context: Post-Paris Agreement actions include coal restrictions, renewable financing targets, a 2020 common portfolio alignment methodology, and 2021 NZBA founding membership; objective to align financing of highest-emitting sectors with net-zero by 2050 consistent with 1.5°C.
- Governance and adaptability: Transition plan assumptions, data, and methodologies may evolve; ongoing reassessments (new exercise launched end-2024, completion expected Q2 2025).

nodes.title: Climate transition plan
nodes.heading: 5.3.2 Climate transition plan
nodes.start_phrase: The COP 21 summit in Paris in 2015 marked an important turning point in the fight against climate change on a global scale.
nodes.summary:
- Defines business risk and how climate-related transition and physical risks are considered material over short, medium and long terms; budgeting incorporates a “Below 2°C” scenario. Notes potential impacts from policy/regulatory shifts and stakeholder behavior, and highlights climate-related financing opportunities.
- Introduces Societe Generale’s climate transition plan post‑COP21: progressive tightening of fossil-fuel policies, portfolio alignment with the Paris Agreement, and NZBA membership targeting net‑zero by 2050 (1.5°C).
- Scope and levers of the plan:
  - Corporate financing: align portfolios in the highest‑emitting sectors with Paris‑aligned trajectories; reduce fossil‑fuel financing and support sector decarbonisation.
  - Life insurance: align invested assets with Paris goals via the Net‑Zero Asset Owner Alliance.
- Alignment methodology and scenarios:
  - Five‑step internal process (baseline, roadmap, action plan, transparent reporting, operationalisation).
  - Prefer IEA NZE 2050 scenario; use sector‑specific science‑based scenarios where needed; updateable as science evolves.
  - Focus on 12 high‑emitting sectors (targets for 10), covering ~73% of corporate Scope 1–2 financed emissions; progress tracked in NZBA reports.
- Sector targets and approaches:
  - Target types: exposure/absolute emissions (coal, oil and gas), physical intensity (power, cement, aluminium, automotive, aviation, commercial real estate), and alignment scores (steel, shipping).
  - Key policy stances and examples:
    - Thermal coal: no new project financing since 2016; full exit by 2030 (EU/OECD) and 2040 (rest of world).
    - Oil & gas: no Arctic/oil sands; reduce upstream exposure by 80% by 2030 (vs. 2019); absolute financed emissions reduction; stop dedicated financing for greenfield projects; strengthen methane and flaring criteria; phase out upstream pure players; restrictions on FPSOs.
    - Power, cement, steel, aluminium, automotive, shipping, aviation, commercial real estate: sector‑specific intensity/alignment targets using frameworks like PACTA, SSP, SAFF, Poseidon Principles, Pegasus Guidelines, CRREM; acknowledge data limits and assumptions.
- Execution and governance:
  - Integration via ESG by Design into budgeting, training and decision‑making; cross‑functional oversight by Finance, Risk and Sustainability; Board approval (March 6, 2025); ongoing disclosure (Climate & Alignment Report; NZBA Progress Report).
- Transition finance commitment:
  - Contribute ~EUR 500bn to sustainable finance by 2030 (EUR ~400bn financing/advisory; EUR ~100bn sustainable bonds; ~80% environmental/20% social), focused on low‑carbon energy, sustainable real estate, mobility, industry transition.
  - “The Shift” programme builds sectoral expertise and solutions across value chains (renewables, hydrogen, CCUS, low‑carbon materials, batteries/charging, shipping fuels, building efficiency).
  - Development of a business transition assessment tool for client engagement and portfolio steering.
  - Partnerships to shape common standards and comparability (Poseidon Principles, Hydrogen Council, SSP, SAFF, Pegasus, Getting to Zero).
  - Innovation ecosystem: investments in Reed – Societe Generale Group (EUR 1bn envelope; EUR 250m initial fund), EIT InnoEnergy, and Partech growth impact fund.
- Life insurance alignment (Societe Generale Assurances):
  - EUR 146bn AUM (end‑2024); NZAOA member; intermediate target to cut equity/corporate bond portfolio footprint by 30% by 2025 vs 2018 already exceeded (-66% by 2023).
  - Measures: fossil‑fuel exclusions (coal exit by 2030/2040), reduce upstream oil & gas exposure by 80% (2020–2030; interim -50% by 2025), and double sustainable assets (goal achieved; ~EUR 7bn on balance sheet at end‑2024).
  - 2024 status: coal exposure ~1% (0.01% when weighted by coal share); ongoing definition of 2030 target; reporting under Article 29.
- Management of material climate impacts:
  - Environmental & Social (E&S) General Principles and sector‑specific policies (industrial agriculture/forestry, mining, oil & gas, thermal power, thermal coal, shipping) guide exclusions, assessments and best practices; Equator Principles applied to relevant project finance.
  - Continuous updates via stakeholder dialogue; proportional due diligence; for Assurances, ESG integration in investments (issuer rating thresholds) and controversy management.

nodes.title: Management of material impacts on climate change mitigation
nodes.heading: 5.3.3 Management of material impacts on climate change mitigation
nodes.start_phrase:
The management of potential impacts on climate change is based on 
the general framework for identifying and preventing serious 
environmental and social (E&S) impacts, the implementation of which 
is inseparable from the processes governing the conduct of the Group’s 
activities.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Societe Generale Group’s framework for managing material impacts on climate change mitigation within its Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) agenda, including policies, governance, tools, actions, training, and greenhouse gas (GHG) reporting.

- E&S General Principles and Equator Principles:
  - Group‑wide framework to identify, assess, prevent, and mitigate environmental and social (E&S) impacts, including climate.
  - Publicly available General E&S Principles guide client and transaction assessments.
  - Equator Principles applied to relevant project finance and related corporate loans with tailored due diligence.

- Sector‑specific policies (public, regularly updated, approved by General Management; shaped by stakeholder dialogue):
  - Common structure with three criteria types: exclusions; priority assessment criteria (with improvement timeframes/action plans); other assessment criteria.
  - Coverage includes industrial agriculture and forestry; mining; oil & gas; thermal power stations; thermal coal; shipping.
  - Proportionate application based on inherent E&S risks; integrated into controversy analysis and client/transaction reviews.

- Key structural criteria by sector:
  - Oil & Gas: end of financial products/services for new greenfield upstream projects and associated infrastructure; phased withdrawal from upstream pure‑players; client exclusion if >30% revenues from listed fossil resources; tighter rules on LNG (no new fields/associated infra; restrictions on shale and Arctic gas); client expectations on methane leak detection/intensity targets, flaring elimination by 2030, direct emissions monitoring, and climate governance.
  - Mining: exclusion of Mountain Top Removal; exclusion of clients with >50% revenues from metallurgical coal; no dedicated transactions tied to metallurgical coal or related infrastructure.
  - Thermal power stations: criteria on GHG intensity/efficiency and air pollutants; new plants must meet national/international standards; fuel/intensity conditions (e.g., CCGT cap); coal‑specific exclusions handled under Thermal Coal policy.
  - Thermal coal: exclusion of developers and clients without phase‑out dates aligned with Group 2030 (EU/OECD)/2040 (RoW) exit; revenue‑based thresholds; dedicated transaction bans for mining, transport, trading, processing, and coal‑fired generation/infrastructure; transition‑only financing exception for non‑compliant clients.
  - Shipping: client strategies aligned with IMO GHG targets with quantitative goals and emissions reporting; exclusion of ships for Arctic oil, tar sands, coal, and single‑hull; MARPOL compliance; Poseidon Principles data; efficiency checks and mitigation plans for second‑hand ships.
  - Industrial agriculture and forestry: protect soils; rational pesticide/fertiliser use; deforestation limits with targeted exclusions; specific focus on South American soy and beef and palm oil (zero‑deforestation commitments by end‑2025), extended assessment to cocoa, coffee, rubber, and timber; exclusions for impacts on High Carbon Stock areas, large‑scale slash‑and‑burn, soy and cattle in Amazon/Cerrado.

- Societe Generale Assurances (SGA) policies and ESG integration:
  - ESG criteria embedded in investments via Amundi (excludes new investments with lowest ESG ratings; case‑by‑case for low ratings).
  - Thermal coal: exclusion of direct investments in companies tied to coal mining, >5 GW coal capacity, major coal producers, developers, or those without 2030/2040 coal phase‑out commitments.
  - Oil & gas: no financing of new exploration/production projects; exclusion thresholds for unconventional fossil fuels (5% new, 10% existing holdings); stop new direct investments in companies that continue to develop new oil/gas projects; can invest via renewable‑only subsidiaries or green bonds to support transition.
  - Engagement via Amundi: proactive stewardship on low‑carbon transition with escalation (rating downgrades, AGM questions, votes against, public statements, score caps, issuer bans); coverage of issuers responsible for most portfolio emissions.

- Impact management framework and controls:
  - Three stages: E&S identification (exclusion and identification lists; negative news screening; integration into financial security tools); E&S assessment (controversy policy since June 2022; time‑horizon aligned to financing; positive/conditional/negative opinions); E&S actions (contractual conditions, monitoring, restrictions, exits).
  - Second line reviews by Risk/Compliance; escalation to Group committees (Client Acceptance; Complex Transactions & Reputational Risks).
  - SGA portfolio ESG assessments by Amundi and Sustainalytics; three lines of defence and dedicated committees for arbitration.

- Implementation and recent enhancements (2024–2025):
  - Expanded E&S exclusion list and formal withdrawal procedures; automated controversy monitoring; materiality grids; strengthened control points on policy exclusions and E&S assessments; Compliance standards controls and indicators.
  - Highest‑emitting sectors under NZBA: governance and processes for periodic monitoring of alignment indicators; new published alignment target for aviation; ongoing work for agriculture and residential real estate.
  - Sector policy update (Oct 2024): Industrial Agriculture & Forestry—zero‑deforestation by end‑2025 for South American soy/beef and palm oil; extended criteria to cocoa, coffee, rubber, timber.
  - SGA actions: deployment of ESG data tool (ESG Connect); tighter coal exclusions (including halting investments in energy producers without public coal phase‑out by 2030/2040); accelerated oil & gas exit targets (‑50% by 2025 vs 2020; ‑80% by 2030).

- ESG training:
  - Group‑wide e‑learning available in 11 languages; >150 ESG modules (e‑learning, MOOCs, workshops, master classes, podcasts); tiered skill paths (≥5 hours fundamentals; >50 hours expert tracks).

- Greenhouse gas emissions reporting (GHG Protocol aligned):
  - Definitions and use of primary/secondary data; consolidation under operational control.
  - Total ~79 MtCO2e (excluding counterparties’ scope 3), mainly:
    - ~41 MtCO2e from corporate financing and life‑insurance investments.
    - ~34 MtCO2e from Ayvens mobility/leasing, accounted over vehicle lifecycles: category 2 (manufacture of purchased vehicles), category 13 (use during lease), and category 11 (post‑lease remaining life), with category 11 representing >40% of leasing‑related emissions.

nodes.title: Greenhouse gas emissions attributed to the Group
nodes.heading: 5.3.4 Greenhouse gas emissions attributed to the Group
nodes.start_phrase:
A scope is a category of greenhouse gas emissions within the carbon footprint of human or corporate activity, determined by the nature of the 
emissions:
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Societe Generale Group’s 2024 greenhouse gas accounting, methodological perimeter, key Scope 3 components (including financed and leasing-related emissions), data quality/uncertainties, and the Group’s climate risk management framework.
- Standards and protocols: Carbon footprint compiled under the GHG Protocol; use of ESRS concepts and PCAF Part A for financed emissions; portfolio emissions estimated by S&P Trucost using the EVIC approach.
- Data types: Distinguishes primary data (collected by the Group/suppliers) and secondary data (sector averages, estimates, proxies). Emission factors mainly from ADEME, IEA/AIE, DEFRA, and specialized providers.
- Organizational and operational scope:
  - Consolidates entities under operational control; for own operations and upstream value chain, covers 197 entities ≥10 employees (≈98.7% of staff).
  - Downstream scope calculated case by case; Ayvens (car leasing/mobility) is the only entity in categories 11 and 13; investments/financed emissions in category 15 include life-insurance assets.
- 2024 carbon footprint headline figures (excluding counterparties’ Scope 3):
  - Scope 1: 42,867 tCO2e (0% under regulated ETS).
  - Scope 2: 110,878 tCO2e (location-based) and 70,108 tCO2e (market-based).
  - Scope 3 total: 79,278,756 tCO2e; total GHG ≈79.4 MtCO2e (location-based).
  - Major Scope 3 contributors:
    - Category 15 Investments: 44.2 MtCO2e.
    - Ayvens-related emissions across the vehicle life cycle: manufacturing (Cat. 2: 10.17 Mt), downstream leased assets (Cat. 13: 9.81 Mt), use of sold products (Cat. 11: 14.35 Mt) — together ≈34 Mt, covering full vehicle lifetime, not just leasing.
    - Other published categories: Purchased goods/services (0.59 Mt), Business travel (0.036 Mt), Employee commuting (0.096 Mt).
  - Several Scope 3 categories deemed not relevant are not published (3.3, 3.4, 3.5, 3.8–3.10, 3.12, 3.14).
- Calculation methods and notes:
  - Scope 1: Fuel consumption converted using ADEME factors; business trips in Group-owned ICE cars included.
  - Scope 2: Location-based uses grid average factors; market-based uses supplier certificates/labels, residual mix, green tariffs; uncertified supplier data excluded.
  - Purchased goods/services and capital goods: Spend-based approach with ADEME monetary emission factors; 9 months of data extrapolated to 12.
  - Business travel and commuting: Mix of provider data and standard emission factors; commuting includes work-from-home emissions.
  - Ayvens vehicle emissions: Uses manufacturer data; DEFRA factors where missing; lifetime assumptions 12–14 years depending on powertrain.
- Investments (Scope 3, Category 15) perimeter and methodology:
  - Included: Listed equities, corporate bonds, corporate loans to non-financial sectors, and life-insurance savings assets under management.
  - Excluded: Mortgage loans, car purchase loans, and sovereign debt.
  - Financed emissions: Calculated per PCAF for non-financial corporates using a hierarchy of data (client-reported, provider-estimated, then PCAF factors); attribution via an AUM-to-client-capital structure ratio.
  - Insurance-related investment emissions: Estimated by S&P Trucost (Scope 1–3), EVIC-based, covering euro fund and unit-linked portfolios; upstream Scope 3 fully modelled.
  - Separate disclosure (not in the main totals) of counterparties’ own absolute emissions as required by PCAF:
    - Financed emissions counterparties: Scope 1+2 = 41.69 Mt; Scope 3 = 116.42 Mt; 22% primary data.
    - Insurance-related counterparties: Scope 1+2 = 2.52 Mt; Scope 3 = 19.84 Mt; primary data share ~9% (euro fund) and ~13% (unit-linked).
- Uncertainties and limitations:
  - Scope 3 inherently uncertain; supplier data gaps; reliance on averages and proxies; potential double counting challenges across categories.
  - Categories 6 and 7 not fully covering all entities; several downstream figures based on secondary data.
  - First-time sustainability statement publication for Category 15 with sectoral interpretation challenges; continuous improvement planned for data quality and timelines.
- Climate risk management framework:
  - ESG risks integrated into the Group’s existing risk processes (identification, quantification, risk appetite, monitoring, reporting, control, mitigation).
  - Mitigation vs adaptation: Defined per CSRD; in finance, both feed into understanding transition and physical risks to counterparties; resilience factors (e.g., protections, insurance) considered.
  - Scenario analysis: Uses a central Below 2°C (B2D), a stressed transition NZE 2050, and a high-emissions physical risk scenario (Current Policies, CP); horizons of 1 year, 5 years, and long term (2040–2050).
  - Environmental Vulnerability Indicators: Assess counterparties (sovereigns, industries, corporates) across climate, biodiversity, water, pollution, and circularity; used in stress tests, portfolio monitoring, and targeted mitigation, with emphasis on trajectories to 2030 and beyond to 2050.

nodes.title: Climate Risk Management
nodes.heading: 5.3.5 Climate Risk Management
nodes.start_phrase:
ESG factors are incorporated into the Group’s risk management 
framework, particularly in relation to climate change‑related risks.
nodes.summary:
- Disclosures under PCAF: The Group publishes separate absolute Scope 1–2 and Scope 3 emissions of counterparties for loans and investments, as well as insurance-related emissions, noting ongoing improvements to Scope 3 data quality and processes.
- Climate risk management embedded in the risk framework: ESG/climate risks are integrated across identification, quantification, risk appetite, monitoring, reporting, control, and mitigation, with references to broader ESG governance.
- Mitigation vs adaptation: While aligned with CSRD definitions, the bank focuses on financial materiality—mitigation linking to transition risk and adaptation to physical risk and counterparties’ resilience/insurance.
- Scenario-based quantification: Use of a central Below 2°C (B2D) scenario, a stressed transition NZE 2050 scenario, and a stressed physical Current Policies scenario over short (1y), medium (5y), and long (2040–2050) horizons.
- Climate vulnerability indicators on an 11-point scale (−5 to +5):
  - ICVI (industry-level, 114 segments) for transition and physical risk, used in credit and counterparty stress tests.
  - CCVI (company-level), enhancing ICVI with a climate strategy questionnaire; rolled out first to most exposed counterparties and integrated into internal credit ratings.
  - SCVI (sovereign-level) for transition and physical risk; sovereign climate risk not deemed material for the Group.
- Stress testing: Progressive integration of climate risk into enterprise-wide stress tests; dedicated methodology described elsewhere.
- Physical risk integration: Enhanced asset location data collection, external hazard scoring tools, and improved understanding via Pillar 3 disclosures.
- Credit loss estimation: ESG factors (ICVI/CCVI) inform ratings; sector-specific overlays adjust expected credit losses through governed processes that integrate climate considerations.
- ICAAP: Gradual strengthening of climate/environmental risk incorporation into capital adequacy from both regulatory and internal risk perspectives.
- Risk appetite: Climate and environmental risks included since 2022; strengthened indicators for sector-level alignment and exposure, governance escalation, and potential portfolio limits (e.g., coal).
- Control and mitigation tools:
  - Allocation/monitoring guidelines requiring exclusion-list checks, sector policy compliance, CCVI review, and controversy assessment.
  - Environmental and social exclusion lists and internal identification lists to flag high-controversy areas early.
  - Sector policies across 10 sectors with exclusion/evaluation criteria.
  - Negative news screening; in-depth ESG due diligence for clients/transactions; climate considerations in New Product Committees.
- Strategic alignment:
  - NZBA sector alignment targets for 10 high-emitting sectors (Oil & Gas, Thermal Coal, Power, Cement, Steel, Aluminium, Automotive, Shipping, Commercial Real Estate, Aviation) with monitoring and public progress reporting.
  - Business Environment Scan to embed climate/environmental risks and opportunities into business strategy, with Risk function challenge.
- Collateral and insurance:
  - ESG factors embedded in collateral valuation; Group-wide collection and use of Energy Performance Certificates (EPC) in lending decisions.
  - Recognition that climate damage insurance may become less comprehensive/selective as extreme events intensify.
- Counterparty and business risk mitigants: Margining and contractual mitigants for counterparty risk; focus on hedging products and clearing; business risk mitigated via transition commitments and annual strategic adequacy assessments.
- Data management: Multi-source ESG data with ongoing expansion of providers, proxies where needed, enhanced quality controls, and system integration. Improvements include EPC data flows, better financed-asset location coverage for physical risk, and incremental Green Asset Ratio refinements. Initial outputs from upgraded data architecture expected from 2025 onward.
- Climate-related opportunities:
  - Material current and medium-term revenues from supporting client transition.
  - Corporate & Investment Banking: Client transition analysis tools; financing energy efficiency, sobriety, renewables, storage, and low-carbon transport; green/social/sustainability-linked financing; transition-focused trade finance.
  - Retail banking (France and international): Advisory on carbon footprint and subsidies; financing for renovations, new builds, and renewables; support for SMEs, corporates, institutions, and emerging transition players.

nodes.title: Material climate change ‑related opportunities
nodes.heading: 5.3.6 Material climate change ‑related opportunities
nodes.start_phrase: The Group identifies many short- and medium‑term opportunities in supporting its clients to move towards a low‑carbon transition.
nodes.summary:
- Focus on environmental opportunities tied to climate change: Societe Generale identifies material short- and medium-term revenue opportunities from supporting clients’ low‑carbon transitions, with significant current and projected ESG-related revenues, especially in financing.
- Corporate and Investment Banking initiatives: A Global Banking & Investor Solutions program collaborates with clients to design transition solutions and uses a tool to assess clients’ transition strategies and related financing needs.
- 2024 financing and advisory activities: Funding for energy efficiency and sobriety (renovations, new builds, improved energy production/distribution, low‑carbon freight), and renewable energy (wind, photovoltaic generation, transmission, distribution, storage). Expansion of green, social, and sustainability loans, plus Sustainability‑Linked products that tie financing costs to clients’ ESG performance. Trade finance developed offerings for renewable energy and clean transport.
- Retail banking opportunities: Strong financing demand from corporate, SME, and institutional clients for ecological transition. In France, services include carbon footprint assessments, subsidy support, financing of transformation projects, ecosystem building, tech development, and support for emerging transition players. Internationally, opportunities span real estate (new construction, energy renovations) and renewable energy financing.
- Social information—responsible employer: The Group manages Human Capital through policies and tools to attract, recruit, integrate, train, and engage employees; Human Capital includes employees and non‑employees working on the Group’s behalf (excluding value‑chain service providers).
- Workforce overview: Operations in 60+ countries with about 119,000 employees. Regional headcount as of 31 Dec 2024: Europe 92,227; Asia 13,567; Africa 9,260; Americas 3,480; Oceania 63.
- Data methodology: Employee scope includes permanent and fixed‑term contracts (incl. work‑study). Gender reporting currently limited to women and men. Data sourced from Group HR systems with local inputs; figures are headcount (not FTE) for FY2024; consolidated scope covers entities with 10+ employees included in the 2024 social information campaign.

nodes.title: SOCIAL INFORMATION
nodes.heading: 5.4 SOCIAL INFORMATION

- Focus: The Group’s approach to responsible employer practices in human capital management, covering attraction, recruitment, integration, training, and employee engagement.

nodes.title: Own workforce
nodes.heading: 5.4.1 Own workforce
nodes.start_phrase: The Group acts as a responsible employer in the management of Human Capital through all the policies and tools implemented within the company to attract, recruit, integrate, train and engage employees.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and context: Extract from Societe Generale’s 2025 Universal Registration Document (CSR – Social Information) covering “Own workforce” and “Consumers and end-users.”
- Workforce profile and methodology:
  - ~119,000 employees in 60+ countries; 92,227 in Europe; 63 in Oceania.
  - Gender split: 54% women (63,704) and 46% men (54,893).
  - Contracts: 111,754 permanent; 6,843 temporary; 109,682 full‑time; 8,915 part‑time.
  - Data reported at headcount level for the 2024 financial year and consolidated scope (entities with ≥10 employees).
- Human rights and materiality:
  - Alignment with UDHR, ILO core conventions, OECD Guidelines, UNGPs, UNESCO World Heritage Convention.
  - Double materiality identifies potential negative impacts on diversity/equity/inclusion, disability inclusion, training/skills, inappropriate behavior/harassment, health & safety, work‑life balance/privacy, fair compensation, social dialogue, freedom of association/collective bargaining; no material risks on forced or child labor.
- Responsible Employer strategy and governance:
  - Targets for 2026: ≥35% women in Top 250 (Leaders Circle); €100m budget to reduce gender pay gaps.
  - Group-wide policies centralized; quarterly HR monitoring; employee barometer for feedback.
  - Commitments mapped to ESRS topics across pillars: employability and careers; equitable and inclusive culture (incl. disability); work‑life balance and health & safety; social dialogue and rights; solidarity/positive impact.
- Talent, mobility, and skills:
  - Strategic Workforce Planning deployed across BUs/SUs.
  - Internal mobility principles (transparency, fill from within, standardized recruitment).
  - ACE skills platform with AI matching (covering ~65% of employees).
  - Reskilling programs since 2020 (90 programs; 860+ employees; focus on Data, ESG, Agile).
  - Comprehensive training offer (risk/compliance mandatory, data/AI, CSR, leadership, behavioral); average 38.2 training hours/employee in 2024.
  - Performance management cycle (Direct–Mobilise–Review) using a common tool.
  - Turnover: 12.4% for permanent contracts in 2024.
- Diversity, Equity & Inclusion (DE&I):
  - Five priority axes: gender, disability/neurodiversity, ethnic/cultural/socio‑economic origin, intergenerational, LGBTI inclusion.
  - DE&I governance (Deputy CEO sponsorship, DE&I Committee, dedicated team and networks).
  - Public commitments and agreements (UNI Global Union global agreement; national charters/agreements in France).
  - Coverage: 100% employees under a DE&I policy; 98% with local DE&I initiatives.
  - Indicators (2024): 30% women in Top 250; 54.5% women on Executive Committee; 41% women managers; age split 19% <30, 61% 30–50, 20% >50.
  - Disability inclusion actions (agreements, awareness, accessibility, training academy).
- Health, safety, and work‑life balance:
  - Group H&S policy with shared responsibilities (Security, HR/health, managers), global security framework and continuous risk monitoring.
  - Awareness and protection measures (e.g., support after aggression/robbery; travel risk policy).
  - H&S KPIs (2024): 98% coverage; 68% audited; 0 deaths; 631 accidents; frequency rate 2.93.
  - Work‑life balance: compliance with local hours, workload discussions, benefits for caregivers/parents; minimum 14 weeks maternity and 1 week paternity leave via UNI agreement; enhanced parental and chronic illness support in France.
  - Quality of Life at Work agreement in France (2023–2025) on hybrid work, freedom of expression, workload, chronic illness, psychosocial risks.
  - Remote work: 95% of employees covered; standard two days/week in France; 92,268 teleworking at end‑2024.
- Compensation, adequate wage, and pay equity:
  - Gender pay gap (global, gross): 34% average and 22% median gap favoring men (contextualized by role/geography mix); commitment to gender pay neutrality and €100m budget to close gaps.
  - Pay ratios: highest paid to average = 69; highest paid to median = 97.
  - Adequate wage: adoption of Fair Wage Network living wage benchmarks; 2024 analysis identified gaps in three subsidiaries; corrective actions implemented; no remaining gaps to living or statutory/CB minimum wages at end‑2024.
- Social dialogue and representation:
  - Renewed global agreement with UNI Global Union (covers 100% of employees) enhancing union rights and duty of care oversight.
  - Structured staff representation (European Group Committee; Central and local Social & Economic Committees).
  - 191 local agreements in 2024, covering 68% of workforce; in France, 99.9% employee representation; 99.3% rate of entities rating social dialogue good/very good.
- Employee voice, conduct, and incident management:
  - Annual Employee Satisfaction Survey (76% response in 2024); engagement 65%; 88% feel included; 75% good work‑life balance; 83% would whistleblow.
  - Culture & Conduct program (ethics, compliance, speak‑up culture).
  - Anti‑inappropriate behavior policy with zero tolerance; mandatory training; manager and HR workshops.
  - Whistleblowing procedure available to all stakeholders; global disciplinary policy.
  - 2024 outcomes: 310 alerts; 63 confirmed incidents (discrimination, sexist acts, psychological/sexual harassment) with action plans and sanctions; €47k final court‑ordered damages in France; no human rights incidents reported via internal channels or unions.
- Solidarity and employee engagement in society:
  - Skills-based volunteering (three days/year in France), “Move for Youth” challenge (22,000 employees, 62 countries); senior part‑time sponsorship; 11,364 days of solidarity actions by 11,513 employees; support for army reserve with paid leave beyond legal minima in France.
- Consumers and end‑users (customers) – impacts, risks, and policies:
  - Two groups considered: direct customers and customers of financed counterparties.
  - Potential negative impacts: data/privacy breaches; non‑discrimination and access to products/services and to quality information.
  - Identified social risk factor: consumer/end‑user issues can aggravate corporate clients’ credit risk (via litigation, fines, reputational damage, revenue loss).
  - Management framework: Code of Conduct, Global Customer Protection Policy (honest, fair, professional conduct; customer interests first), compliance systems, disciplinary policy, and periodic human rights and safety risk assessments.

nodes.title: Consumers and end users
nodes.heading: 5.4.2 Consumers and end users
nodes.start_phrase: A distinction should be made between two types of consumers and end‑users within the Group: direct customers of the Group’s products and services, and customers of products and services that are provided by counterparties that the Group finances.
nodes.summary:
- Scope and stakeholders: Defines “consumers and end-users” as both Societe Generale’s direct retail and insurance customers and the customers of counterparties financed by the Group.
- Material social impacts and risks:
  - Potential negative impacts on customers include personal data/privacy breaches and risks linked to non-discrimination, access to products/services, and access to quality information, with heightened exposure for vulnerable clients.
  - Consumers/end-users social risk is identified as an aggravating factor of corporate credit risk in the value chain (via reputational/litigation events leading to higher costs and revenue loss); assessed qualitatively over a 10-year horizon.
- Governance, codes, and oversight:
  - Group Code of Conduct, Global Customer Protection Policy, anti-corruption/AML-CFT, conflict-of-interest prevention, and a disciplinary sanctions policy with zero tolerance for misconduct.
  - Regular human rights, freedoms, and health & safety risk identification; adherence to UN Global Compact, OECD Guidelines, UNGPs, and SDGs.
- Customer protection policies:
  - Product governance and customer information duties aligned with MiFID II and IDD; New Products Committees and Product Governance Committees; Board Risk Committee oversight; “Value for money” principle.
  - Focus on KYC-driven advice, suitability, and fair treatment; special protections for vulnerable customers (age, legal capacity, financial precarity).
- Access, non-discrimination, and inclusion:
  - Prohibition of discriminatory practices; “right to an account” support and procedures for referrals by central banks where applicable.
  - Accessibility for people with disabilities: >98% accessible branches (2,083 sites, Oct 2024), adapted ATMs (headphones for visually impaired), braille statements, improved digital ergonomics; commitment to digital accessibility and publication of a Multi‑Year Accessibility Plan.
- Responsible marketing and support for vulnerable clients:
  - Early detection systems for financial vulnerability; capped/ frozen fees; Specific Offering for Financially Vulnerable Customers; lending criteria designed to prevent undue hardship/over‑indebtedness.
  - Clear, accurate, non‑misleading information; expanded disclosures on ESG labels and clients’ sustainability preferences.
  - Complaints handling and mediation framework (updated 2023), with governance, KPIs, and free access to ombudsman; conflict-of-interest management with disclosure where needed (DACI reporting; 2023 policy update).
- Employee requirements:
  - Mandatory training on customer protection; compensation aligned to customer interest, compliance and conduct; appraisals include conduct/compliance; controls against forced selling; mystery shopping; customer satisfaction included in sales force evaluations.
- Privacy and data protection:
  - Banking secrecy and confidentiality obligations; GDPR compliance framework with a Group DPO reporting to Compliance and the Audit & Internal Control Committee; network of local DPOs and regular reporting.
  - High completion of GDPR training (97.8% in 2024); DPIAs where high risk; legal basis reviews; data subject rights handling; breach management; security measures (classification, authentication, encryption, DLP); cross‑border transfer impact assessments and contractual safeguards.
  - Third‑party governance and audits (including CIIG); data records management and archiving policy with integrity, traceability, and access principles; lifecycle data purging.
- Actions to reduce negative impacts:
  - Financial education and inclusion initiatives: expert video series, youth-oriented Boost platform, “1 Jeune 1 Solution,” Boursorama’s Bourso Campus and broad ESG/company information.
  - Philanthropy via the Societe Generale Foundation; support to Crésus and the Dilemme program (~100,000 youths reached in 10 years; international roll‑out).
  - Microfinance support: partnerships with ADIE (EUR 21.5m credit lines, EUR 41.2m outstanding in 2024) and long-standing financing of African MFIs in local currency.
- Inclusive product offerings and over‑indebtedness prevention:
  - France: Generis (1€/month; tools and budget advice) and Kapsul (2€/month; essential services) with 2024 uptake (Generis: 56,092; Kapsul: 6,962).
  - BoursoBank: budget tools (alerts, Wicount), free offering for vulnerable customers with capped incident fees.
  - Centralized support for payment incidents; regional “amicable negotiation/special cases” services (18,000+ cases since 2023; 72% return to branch in 2024); Incident Prevention Service (Concilian) contacts at 60 days overdraft/first unpaid loan.
  - Complaints and mediation 2024 (SG Network France): 6,671 mediation requests; 4,003 admissible; 951 decisions.
- Engagement and remediation:
  - Dialogue via stakeholder engagement and complaint channels; participation in the Observatory of Banking Inclusion (OIB).
  - Mechanisms include complaints/mediation, over‑indebtedness prevention, and financial education.
- Customer satisfaction monitoring:
  - NPS and customer experience embedded in CEO variable compensation; Board oversight.
  - Ongoing listening at SG Network: >50,000 monthly feedback from individuals/professionals, >2,200 quarterly from companies; annual competitive benchmark (CSA, ~15,000 respondents); social channel “SG & Vous” (~6,000 messages/month).
  - Societe Generale Assurances: cold NPS, on‑the‑spot NPS, journey NPS, and digital satisfaction tracking; omnichannel improvements and personalization.
  - International surveys (Czech Republic, Romania, Morocco, Algeria, Côte d’Ivoire, Senegal, Cameroon): stable NPS at KB; sharp increase at BRD; Sub‑Saharan Africa banks remain in top third.
- Integration of social risk into credit:
  - Social criteria (including consumer/end‑user risks) are included in ESG risk analysis within the credit approval process to mitigate related material financial risks.
- Business conduct and corporate culture:
  - Board-led governance of ethics, compliance, AML/CFT, GDPR, reputational risk, customer protection, and whistleblowing; Risk and Audit & Internal Control Committees’ regular reviews; Nomination & Corporate Governance Committee addresses culture.
  - Culture anchored in four values—Team Spirit, Innovation, Commitment, Responsibility—articulated in a Leadership Model with behaviors assessed in annual objectives across all employee levels.

nodes.title: BUSINESS CONDUCT INFORMATION

nodes.title: Management of material impacts related to business conduct
nodes.heading: 5.5.1 Management of material impacts related to business conduct
