nodes.summary:
- Scope and focus: Excerpt from Societe Generale’s 2025 Universal Registration Document (CSR section) detailing Business Conduct Information, including governance of ethics, whistleblowing, anti‑corruption, supplier relations, and how business conduct risks feed into credit risk.
- Governance and culture:
  - Board oversight with defined roles for the Risk Committee (compliance/culture indicators, AML/CFT), Audit and Internal Control Committee (customer protection, market integrity, GDPR, compliance incidents), and Nomination and Corporate Governance Committee (corporate culture).
  - Corporate culture anchored in four values (Team Spirit, Innovation, Commitment, Responsibility) and a Leadership Model embedded in objective‑setting and performance management.
  - Code of Conduct applied group‑wide, aligned with international standards (UDHR, ILO, OECD Guidelines, UNGPs, UNESCO convention), covering confidentiality, market integrity, conflicts of interest, stakeholder relations, and financial crime (AML/CFT, anti‑corruption, tax evasion).
  - Culture and Conduct governance strengthened in 2024 with a Group Head of Culture and Conduct; integration via BU/SU roadmaps, HR levers (conduct in evaluations, disciplinary policy with right to make mistakes), and regular maturity reviews and indicators reported up to the Executive Committee and Board.
- Incident handling and training:
  - Multiple channels for identifying conduct incidents (management, controls, whistleblowing); investigations by expert teams with committee oversight (Compliance Incident Committee; Audit and Internal Control Committee); annual Culture and Conduct reporting to the Board.
  - Expanded mandatory training on ethics and conduct (Code of Conduct, dialogue culture, whistleblowing), complementing risk trainings (anti‑corruption, AML/CFT, market abuse, etc.).
- Whistleblower protection:
  - Group system (WhistleB external platform) available internally and publicly, compliant with French Sapin 2/Waserman and EU Directive 2019/1937, and duty of vigilance law.
  - Open to employees, management, shareholders, business partners, and related stakeholders; strict confidentiality/anonymity; zero retaliation policy.
  - Annual awareness and manager‑specific training; secure, need‑to‑know investigation process with corrective actions.
- Anti‑corruption framework:
  - Zero‑tolerance stance; participation in Wolfsberg Group and UN Global Compact.
  - Internal Code on the fight against corruption and influence peddling embedded in rules; identification of “Most Exposed Persons” (governing bodies, sales, purchasing, notarial power, interest representatives).
  - Prevention/detection pillars: Code of Conduct; risk mapping; targeted training; third‑party due diligence; accounting controls; control framework; disciplinary regime; whistleblowing.
  - Third‑party screening and periodic reviews; incident governance with escalation to executive bodies, Board Risk Committee, and supervisors where relevant.
  - Supporting tools: GEMS (gifts/hospitality), WhistleB, DACI (conflicts of interest), OSERIS (risky ledger entries), MyP&P (standards deployment).
  - Structured training plan for all staff, at‑risk roles, ABC specialists, Board Directors, and Finance/Accounting, with broad coverage and recurring refresh cycles.
  - No convictions or fines for corruption in 2024.
- Supplier relations and responsible sourcing:
  - Sourcing Function, led by the Group Head of Sourcing, operationalizes CSR in procurement and upholds the Duty of Care Plan while promoting positive‑impact sourcing.
  - Recognized with France’s Responsible Supplier Relations Label (ISO 20400 basis).
  - E&S risk mapping across 150+ procurement subcategories; higher‑risk areas include building works, waste management, and telecom/IT equipment.
  - Risk management embedded in tenders (E&S criteria and weightings), Know Your Supplier checks (including E&S exclusion list), extra‑financial assessments by third parties, controversy monitoring for ~600 targeted suppliers, contractual CSR clauses, and on‑site audits with remedial action plans when needed.
  - Training for buyers on responsible sourcing; Supplier Relationship Management program; CSR objectives included in buyer performance evaluations.
- Payment practices:
  - Commitment to responsible payment terms formalized in internal rules, supplier contracts, and public information.
  - Process improvements via invoice digitization and “No PO, No Pay” policy; differentiated channels to support SMEs/sensitive suppliers; prioritization based on invoice age/supplier situation.
  - Reported metrics (overheads scope ~83% of Group): Group average payment time 31 days with 89% of payments aligned with practices; selected country breakdowns provided; five ongoing late‑payment proceedings in 2024.
- Management of material risks related to business conduct:
  - Governance risk identified as a significant aggravating factor for credit risk to corporate counterparties/financial institutions, with pathways via compliance, reputational, and litigation exposures.
  - Mitigation through integration of governance into ESG risk analysis within credit approvals; robust financial security processes (KYC, controversy monitoring, PEP/sanctions screening, transaction monitoring); and use of E&S exclusion and identification lists to condition or restrict engagements.
- Cybersecurity:
  - Referenced to Risk Management and Operational Risk chapters for organization, monitoring, and measurement details.

nodes.title: REPORT ON THE CERTIFICATION OF SUSTAINABILITY INFORMATION
nodes.heading: 5.7 REPORT ON THE CERTIFICATION OF SUSTAINABILITY INFORMATION
nodes.start_phrase:

under Article 8 of Regulation (EU) 2020/852 of the Company issued in French and it is provided solely for the convenience of English‑speaking users.
nodes.summary:
- Statutory Auditors’ limited assurance report on Société Générale’s 2024 sustainability information and EU Taxonomy (Article 8) disclosures, included in the 2025 Universal Registration Document (CSR chapter), prepared under French law, ESRS, and H2A limited assurance guidelines.
- Scope of engagement:
  - Compliance of the process used to determine sustainability information with ESRS, including stakeholder identification, identification and assessment of impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs), and impact/financial materiality assessment; verification of the legal requirement to consult the social and economic committee.
  - Compliance of the sustainability information disclosed with Article L.233‑28‑4 of the French Commercial Code, including ESRS.
  - Compliance with EU Taxonomy Article 8 disclosure requirements (eligibility/alignment and presentation rules).
- Nature of work: interviews, document reviews, consistency checks, and targeted testing; procedures calibrated for limited assurance (not reasonable assurance), no opinion on strategy viability, ambition of targets, or relevance of choices; comparative information not covered; no conclusions on isolated elements.
- Key conclusions:
  - No material errors, omissions, or inconsistencies identified in the ESRS process used to determine reported information.
  - Social and economic committee consultation had not yet been held at the report date (noted without modifying the conclusion).
  - No material errors, omissions, or inconsistencies identified in the sustainability information’s compliance with Article L.233‑28‑4 and ESRS.
  - No material errors, omissions, or inconsistencies identified regarding compliance with EU Taxonomy Article 8 requirements.
- Emphases of matter (limitations and methodological notes, without qualification of conclusions):
  - Transition plan scope and financed emissions scope (Scope 3, category 15) and related data/methodology/assumptions limitations.
  - EU Taxonomy methodology and retail customer alignment measurement choices and limitations.
- Areas of particular attention and procedures:
  - ESRS process: validation of stakeholder mapping consistency; review of IRO identification across own operations and value chain with time horizons; assessment of materiality methodology against ESRS 1.
  - Greenhouse gas disclosures (sections 5.3.4 and 5.3.2): review of internal controls; for financed emissions (Scope 3 categories 11, 13, 15), checks of calculation scopes vs consolidated balance sheet, emission factors, conversions, extrapolations, sectoral proxies, and arithmetic accuracy; for own operations (Scope 3 categories 1, 2, 6, 7), review of inventory approach, factors, conversions, source data, and calculations.
  - Transition plan for climate change mitigation: assessed disclosure against ESRS E1 and alignment with Group commitments/strategic plan (without opining on ambition).
  - EU Taxonomy Article 8: verification of eligibility/alignment determination process, readability/understandability of presentation, and absence of material misstatements on a risk‑based sample.
- Report signed by PricewaterhouseCoopers Audit and KPMG SA, dated 12 March 2025.

- Mapping of inherent E&S risks (5.8.2):

- Employee risk mapping (updated 2024):

  - Five themes assessed: freedom of association/collective bargaining; discrimination; occupational health and safety; working conditions; human rights.
  - Workforce exposure (Verisk Maplecroft, financial sector lens) shows a majority in low to medium risk countries across all themes, with some high-risk exposure and no “very high” exposure reported under this methodology:

    - Occupational health and safety: Low 71.42%, Medium 18.52%, High 10.06%, Very high 0%

Differences between ITUC and Verisk Maplecroft attributed largely to sectoral vs. country approaches; discussed with UNI Global Union (Dec 2024–Jan 2025).
  - Madagascar entity excluded due to 2024 sale.

- Data sources:
  - HR: Verisk Maplecroft
  - Activities: Verisk Maplecroft and ENCORE

nodes.title: Mapping of inherent E&S risks: identification, analysis and classification of risks
nodes.heading: 5.8.2 Mapping of inherent E&S risks: identification, analysis and classification of risks
nodes.start_phrase:
Societe Generale periodically conducts exercises to identify the risks of 
violations of human rights, fundamental freedoms, health, safety and 
security, and the environment that are inherent in its activities 
(referred to as “inherent E&S risks” ).
nodes.summary:
- Scope and purpose: Extract from Societe Generale’s Universal Registration Document 2025 (CSR, Duty of Care Plan) detailing how the Group identifies, analyzes, classifies, and regularly reassesses inherent environmental and social (E&S) risks across three sub-scopes—employees, suppliers and subcontractors, and the Group’s activities—and the procedures used to manage and monitor these risks.

- Methodology and data sources:
  - Uses recognized external databases and internal expertise, notably Verisk Maplecroft (sector- and country-level human rights and labor risk), ENCORE for natural capital dependencies/pressures, and (for sourcing) Transparency International, World Bank, ILO, UNICEF.
  - Additional analysis on freedom of association and collective bargaining using ITUC Index; differences vs. Verisk Maplecroft discussed with UNI Global Union due to sector vs. country approaches.
  - Distinguishes inherent vs. residual risk; prioritization considers sector, geography, and exposure.

- Employees (updated 2024):
  - Five themes mapped: freedom of association/collective bargaining, discrimination, occupational health and safety, working conditions, human rights.
  - Majority of workforce operates in countries rated low or medium inherent E&S risk; no “very high” risk countries under the financial-sector lens used. Higher “high risk” shares appear for human rights (17.27%), working conditions (10.99%), and OHS (10.06%).
  - Country lists identify where medium/high risks apply by theme (e.g., China often high; multiple African countries; some Americas/Asia/Europe entries; USA appears as medium in several themes).
  - Madagascar entity excluded following its 2024 sale.

- Suppliers and subcontractors:
  - Category-based risk mapping (150+ sub-categories) across three pillars: ethics/compliance, environment, and human rights/labor, with contextual supply chain complexity and labor intensity.
  - Mapping co-developed with three other French banks (2018) and updated; cross-referenced with spend to prioritize action.
  - Spend exposure: approx. 9.62% in high-risk categories and 9.96% in medium-high risk categories.
  - Highest-risk purchases: building works (construction/renovation/fit-out) and IT equipment.
  - Ayvens (vehicle leasing) highlights manufacturing and maintenance risks (GHG emissions, air pollution, resource use, factory OHS).

- Group’s activities (corporate finance portfolio and Ayvens):
  - Climate: prioritizes sectors with high GHG intensity and Group exposure—power generation; road freight/warehousing/storage; hydrocarbons extraction/production; agriculture/forestry/fishing; metallurgical industry; organic chemistry. For Ayvens, key risks are use-phase vehicle emissions and electricity mix for EV charging.
  - Biodiversity and ecosystems: ENCORE-expanded mapping across 13 pressure factors; high-risk sectors in the portfolio include power generation, mining, hydrocarbons, agriculture/forestry/fishing. For Ayvens, pollution from exhaust (NOx, particulates) and from tyre/brake wear.
  - Human rights: sector- and country-specific mapping (Verisk Maplecroft + exposure) covering working conditions, child/forced labor, water/sanitation, community rights, etc. Highest risks in mining, agriculture, heavy industry, hydrocarbon production, notably in Brazil, Cameroon, China, Côte d’Ivoire, India, Turkey. Results guide risk management actions and continuous improvement.

- Procedures for regular assessment of inherent E&S risks:
  - Governance goal: ensure the framework covers main mapped risks; periodically review to close gaps and strengthen prevention/mitigation.
  - Employees:
    - Annual self-assessments: operational risk control self-assessment and a Planethic Reporting questionnaire on Duty of Care themes (consolidated by HR, covering entities with ≥10 employees).
    - Employee Barometer: annual anonymous Group-wide survey; 2024 focus on collective performance, efficiency, responsibility/future; results drive action plans reported to the Board. Additional local pulse checks (e.g., Ayvens), newcomer surveys.
    - Mandatory annual Ethics and Conduct training includes whistleblowing rights.
  - Suppliers and subcontractors:
    - Normative documentation and tools embedded across sourcing stages; applied by the Group Sourcing Division and, at minimum for high-risk categories, by other countries/functions; phased rollout.
    - Capability building: buyer training on sustainable sourcing and E&S tools; awareness video for occasional buyers.
    - Risk controls in practice: category-level E&S risk mapping; E&S criteria in tenders for medium-high/high-risk categories; E&S criteria in Know Your Supplier (including exclusion list); third-party non-financial assessments for targeted suppliers; systematic monitoring of ESG controversies for ~600 targeted and medium/high-risk suppliers via a dedicated tool (reinforced since 2022).

- Outcome linkage: Results of the three mapping exercises inform targeted actions (referenced in section 5.8.4) and underpin the Group’s continuous improvement in managing environmental and human rights risks.

nodes.title: Procedures for regular assessment of inherent E&S risks
nodes.heading: 5.8.3 Procedures for regular assessment of inherent E&S risks
nodes.start_phrase: The aim of the duty of care approach is to provide an appropriate framework for managing inherent E&S risks.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt outlines Societe Generale Group’s Duty of Care Plan for regularly assessing, preventing, and mitigating inherent Environmental & Social (E&S) risks across employees, suppliers, and business activities. It describes a continually updated risk management framework that is reviewed to detect serious risks not adequately covered and to enhance prevention measures.

Key points covered:
- Regular assessment mechanisms
  - Annual self-assessments, including operational risk control self-assessments and a duty of care questionnaire (Planethic Reporting) on local policies, processes, and controls across five duty of care themes, consolidated by HR for entities with 10+ employees.
  - Ongoing review of the inherent E&S risk framework, escalation to second line of defense, and, where needed, arbitration by a Group Steering Committee chaired by an Executive Committee member.
- Employee engagement and conduct
  - Group-wide “Employee Barometer” (annual, anonymous) to gauge engagement and drive action plans at Business/Service Unit level, submitted to the Board; 2024 focus areas included alignment with Group strategy, operational efficiency, and workplace well‑being. Local pulse and onboarding surveys complement feedback.
  - Mandatory “Ethics and Conduct” training includes a whistleblowing module.
- Supplier and subcontractor risk management
  - Normative documentation and tools embedded in sourcing processes to identify, assess, and manage E&S risks by category and supplier, applied at least to high‑risk categories and being phased in Group‑wide.
  - Measures include E&S risk mapping by category; E&S criteria in tenders for medium‑high/high risk categories; KYS with E&S checks (exclusion list); targeted third‑party non‑financial assessments; and reinforced ESG controversy monitoring for ~600 target or medium/high‑risk suppliers.
  - Strengthened KYS since May 2020 for all significant/sensitive suppliers, both at onboarding and periodically.
  - Ayvens: direct sourcing outside the Group Sourcing Division but aligned via a 2024 Sustainable Sourcing Charter; E&S questionnaires weighted in awards; E&S integrated into KYS.
- E&S risk management in business activities
  - Group normative framework defines roles/responsibilities; E&S considerations integrated into client onboarding, transactional, and periodic review processes.
  - Three-step system:
    1) Identification (E&S exclusion list, E&S identification list, controversies, sector policies, decarbonization targets, and governance due diligence within KYC/AML/CTF/tax).
    2) Assessment (compliance with sector policies and commitments; severity of controversies; Group guidelines since June 2022 for adverse E&S information; issuance of positive/conditional/negative E&S opinions).
    3) Mitigation actions (referenced to section 5.8.4), with phased monitoring/controls by business lines.
  - Deployment of tools to help identify companies in scope of sector policies.
- CSR and E&S training
  - A Group-wide program to build a shared CSR culture and technical expertise, including a multi-level curriculum (5 to 50 hours).
  - By end‑2024, large-scale uptake: 90,500 trained in CSR basics; 82,000 in sustainable finance/regulations; 87,700 on ecological crisis; 91,600 in E&S risk management; 92,000 in Group CSR strategy. 95% of employees took at least one CSR training in 2024.
  - Climate Fresk rolled out to 38% of employees; mandatory E&S risk e‑learning updated in 2023, with ~95% completion among targeted staff by end‑2024; ~32,000 trained on EU sustainable investment regulations.
  - A compulsory online E&S risk module available in 11 languages supports consistent implementation.
  - Entities are accountable for integrating the normative system into their operations; Ayvens is evolving its E&S risk controls post‑merger and accelerating fleet electrification to reduce climate/biodiversity risks.
- Actions to prevent and mitigate serious E&S risks for employees
  - Internal normative documentation (Societe Generale Code) covering human rights and health/safety; a Group Code of Conduct; and thematic policies.
  - Social dialogue, freedom of association, and collective bargaining reinforced by a 2023 global agreement with UNI Global Union (valid four years, covering 100% of the workforce). The agreement strengthens union rights; addresses remote work, digital environment, health/safety/quality of life, anti‑discrimination/harassment, diversity, gender equality, and social protection; and recognizes UNI as a stakeholder consulted annually in the Duty of Care Plan for the employee scope.
  - Anti‑discrimination through a Group‑wide DE&I policy with five priority focuses (gender, disability/neurodiversity, ethnic/cultural/socio‑economic origin, generational inclusion, and LGBT+ inclusion); 100% of employees covered, with 98% of entities running local initiatives in at least one focus.

nodes.title: Actions to prevent and mitigate serious inherent E&S risks
nodes.heading: 5.8.4 Actions to prevent and mitigate serious inherent E&S risks
nodes.start_phrase:
To prevent and mitigate serious inherent E&S risks in its relationships 
with employees, the Societe Generale Group defines specific guidelines 
that cover issues related to human rights, freedom of association and 
collective bargaining rights,
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Extract from Societe Generale’s 2025 Universal Registration Document (CSR – Duty of Care Plan) detailing measures to prevent and mitigate serious inherent environmental and social (E&S) risks across employees, suppliers/subcontractors, and business activities, and describing the Group’s whistleblowing system. Applies to all Group entities and subsidiaries.

- Employees (risk prevention and mitigation):
  - Broad ESG training program with tiered expertise (5–50 hours); by end-2024, large-scale uptake across CSR basics, sustainable finance, ecological crisis, E&S risk management, and CSR strategy; 38% of staff completed the Climate Fresk; 95% took at least one CSR training in 2024; updated mandatory E&S risk e-learning and EU sustainable investment module widely completed.
  - Governance and standards: Group normative framework (“Societe Generale Code”), a global Code of Conduct, and topic-specific policies.
  - Social dialogue and union rights: 2023 renewal of a global agreement with UNI Global Union (covers 100% of workforce), strengthens trade union rights, remote working, digital environment, health/safety, anti-discrimination/anti-harassment, diversity and gender equality, and social protection. UNI recognized as a stakeholder in the Duty of Care Plan.
  - Diversity, Equity & Inclusion: 100% workforce covered; five priority axes (gender, disability/neurodiversity, ethnic/cultural/socio-economic diversity, intergenerational inclusion, LGBT+ inclusion); targets include >35% women in Top 250 by end-2026 and EUR 100m budget to close gender pay gaps by 2026; mandatory non-discrimination training for recruiters; Group-level DE&I governance.
  - Occupational Health & Safety and wellbeing: global health policy adapted locally; France agreement on wellbeing/workplace conditions; prevention of psychosocial risks; 2024 launch of Wellbeing@Work platform and global “wellbeing referents” network; measures to support transformations.
  - Working conditions and data protection: valid employment contracts, equitable and sustainable pay referencing FairWage decent wage guidelines, right to disconnect with flexible hours (covering 90.5% of workforce), and robust employee data/privacy principles.
  - Human rights: minimum hiring age 16, prohibition of forced labor/modern slavery/trafficking, very low exposure to related risks; migrant worker policies in many entities; security of people and assets managed by Group Security (monitoring, standards, supervision/controls, security culture, crisis management).
  - Compliance culture and mandatory trainings: information security, anti-corruption, Code of Conduct, GDPR, sanctions, AML/CFT, conflicts of interest, whistleblowing, anti-harassment; business-line specific training; support materials for “Speak-Up”.

- Suppliers and subcontractors (risk prevention in procurement):
  - E&S requirements embedded in tenders for medium-high/high risk categories globally; E&S criteria weighted in bid evaluations.
  - CSR clauses in contracts including adherence to the Sustainable Sourcing Charter, equivalence to the Group Code of Conduct, audit rights, and non-financial assessments of key suppliers; simplified tools for high-risk procurement outside central sourcing.
  - Remedial action plans encouraged; controversies monitored; on-site E&S audits possible.

- Business activities (E&S risk management and alignment):
  - Sector policies to manage human rights and environmental risks with evaluation and exclusion criteria: industrial agriculture & forestry (deforestation), dams/hydropower (sensitive sites), thermal power and thermal coal (full exit 2030 EU/OECD, 2040 elsewhere), defense (controversial weapons), mining (asbestos and metallurgical coal exclusions for dedicated financing), shipping (various exclusions), civil nuclear, oil & gas (unconventional and new development restrictions), tobacco. 2024 updates strengthened the agriculture/forestry and mining policies for deforestation and human rights.
  - Continued expansion of sector coverage; forthcoming work on organic chemistry and road freight.
  - Operationalization: expanded E&S exclusion list and exit procedures; refined indicators for clients breaching exclusions; controversies integrated into screening tools; KYC rules engine reflects sector policy criteria; harmonized E&S due diligence across entities.

- Climate alignment and portfolio targets (NZBA):
  - Decarbonization targets across top-emitting sectors with transparent reporting (NZBA Progress and Climate & Alignment reports).
  - Key targets: power generation intensity 125 gCO2/kWh by 2030 (-43% vs 2019); oil & gas production exposure -80% by 2030 (-50% by 2025) and financed emissions -70% vs 2019; cement intensity -20% vs 2022; automotive -51% vs 2021; steel aligned with Sustainable Steel Principles (score 0 by 2030); commercial real estate 18 kgCO2e/m² by 2030 (-63% vs 2022); aluminium 6 tCO2e/t (-25% vs 2022); shipping aligned with IMO “Striving For” (≈-43% AER by 2030 vs 2022); commercial aviation 775 gCO2e/RTK by 2030 (-18% vs 2019).
  - Fossil fuel exposure: thermal coal down to <0.1% of loans by end-2023; >50% reduction in oil & gas production exposure by Q2 2024 vs 2019; objectives among most proactive.

- Biodiversity:
  - Strategy aligned with Kunming-Montréal Global Biodiversity Framework and Act4Nature commitments; Group-wide objectives published with assessment due Q1 2025.
  - Risk mapping highlights sensitive sectors; biodiversity risks embedded in E&S framework, sector policies, identification/exclusion lists, and controversies monitoring.
  - Project finance: application of Equator Principles; exclusions for projects in key protected areas and for soy/cattle projects in Amazon/Cerrado.
  - Corporate clients: focus on deforestation risks (soy, cattle, palm oil) with enhanced dialogue on alignment; 2024 analytical work on power sector’s nature impacts; staff training expanded (incl. Biodiversity Fresk).

- Human rights focus in financing:
  - References international standards (UDHR, UNDRIP, ILO, UNESCO WHC, SDGs, UNGPs).
  - Project finance includes human-rights-inclusive E&S assessments, independent reviews, and action plans embedded in financing.

- Whistleblowing procedure:
  - Global, multilingual, secure system compliant with French laws (Sapin II, Waserman) and the Duty of Care law; multiple reporting channels; available to employees, management, directors, shareholders, external/temporary staff, subcontractors, suppliers, and facilitators; protects confidentiality, data, and non-retaliation.
  - 2024 activity: 429 reports (up from 310 in 2023); 159 qualified as legal-scope alerts; ~75% related to human relations (harassment, discrimination); others included corruption, conflicts of interest, data protection; 35% of alerts led to corrective actions, about half with sanctions.
  - Ongoing awareness: prominent access via intranet and website; annual mandatory training for employees; suppliers informed through the Code of Conduct.

nodes.title: Whistleblowing procedure
nodes.heading: 5.8.5 Whistleblowing procedure
nodes.start_phrase: In accordance with the law, the Group has set up a mechanism allowing it to collect alerts (5.1).
nodes.summary:
- Context: Extract from Societe Generale Group’s 2025 Universal Registration Document, Corporate Social Responsibility, Duty of Care Plan.
- Human rights and E&S risk management:
  - Human rights risks integrated into the Group’s overall E&S framework via sectoral policies, E&S Identification and Exclusion Lists, and a controversies monitoring tool.

  - Open to employees, management, Directors, shareholders, external/part‑time staff, subcontractors, suppliers, and facilitators; guarantees confidentiality, data protection, and non‑retaliation; usage guidance in the Code of Conduct.

  - 429 reports via Group tool (vs 310 in 2023); 159 qualified alerts (vs 111).
  - ~75% of alerts concern human relations issues (harassment, sexist acts, discrimination); others relate to corruption, conflicts of interest, data protection, etc.
  - Additional reports via local/managerial/HR channels.
  - 35% of alerts required corrective action; about half of these resulted in sanctions (from reprimand to lay‑off).
- Communication and awareness:
  - Whistleblowing links on intranet and institutional website; annual awareness since 2019; mandatory annual training for all employees.
  - Subcontractors and suppliers informed through the Group’s Code of Conduct.
- Stakeholder dialogue and complaints:
  - Ongoing engagement with NGOs and other stakeholders; relevant third‑party alerts integrated into risk management (e.g., updates to identification lists or sector policies).
  - Comprehensive complaints system available to clients and non‑clients regarding products/services (pricing, advice, service refusal, fraud, regulatory compliance, etc.).
  - Peer exchanges to share best practices; in 2024, focus on emerging AI‑related risks.
- Monitoring and reporting on Duty of Care:
  - Steering/reporting tools deliver extra‑financial KPIs to HR, Security, Sourcing, and Sustainable Development.
  - Internal self‑assessments to monitor E&S process application across units/entities, identify improvements, track action plans, and use additional indicators.
- Employee‑related monitoring and 2024 enhancements:
  - Planethic Reporting questionnaire updated annually; 2024 protocol aligned with CSRD; content reviewed by HR, DEI, and Health & Safety experts.
  - Control environment includes: controls on key HR processes, business continuity plans and crisis exercises, and periodic audits/inspections (including E&S mitigation checks).
  - 2024 actions: collaboration with UNI Global Union—pre‑Board review of the employee section, creation of working groups for ongoing risk analysis/mitigation at local and corporate levels, and a global presentation/discussion post‑publication.
  - Additional initiatives: HR awareness training on duty of care, strengthened psychosocial risk prevention, and workplace design improvements via the Future of Workplace Charter.
- References/notes:
  - Whistleblowing portal link provided; data current as of February 18, 2025.
  - Exceptions noted for sectors the Group has exited.

nodes.title: System for Monitoring duty of care measures and reporting on their effective implementation
nodes.heading: 5.8.6 System for Monitoring duty of care measures and reporting on their effective implementation
nodes.start_phrase: The Group has developed steering and reporting tools to comply with its extra‑financial reporting obligations and monitor implementation of its inherent E&S risk management processes.
nodes.summary:
- Purpose and scope: Extract from Societe Generale’s 2025 Universal Registration Document (CSR, Duty of Care Plan) detailing stakeholder dialogue, monitoring systems, results, and 2025 outlook across employees, suppliers, and core activities.

- Stakeholder dialogue and grievance mechanisms:
  - Ongoing engagement with NGOs and peers to surface E&S issues and emerging risks (notably AI in 2024).
  - Third-party alert channels beyond whistleblowing; integration of relevant alerts into risk management (lists, sector policies).
  - Comprehensive complaints system open to clients and non-clients for all product/service issues.

- Monitoring and reporting framework:
  - Group-wide steering and reporting tools for extra-financial indicators (HR, Security, Sourcing, Sustainable Development).
  - Internal self-assessments to monitor E&S processes in Business/Service Units and legal entities, identify improvements, and track action plans.
  - Annual Planethic Reporting questionnaire refreshed with HR/DE&I/Health & Safety input; 2024 protocol aligned with CSRD.
  - Structured collaboration with UNI Global Union: pre-Board review of employee section, ongoing working groups, and post-publication briefing.

- Employee-related duty of care controls and actions:
  - HR embedded in risk and permanent control systems: key HR process controls, business continuity/crisis exercises, periodic Audit/Inspection.
  - 2024 actions: duty-of-care awareness for HR, strengthened psychosocial risk prevention, workplace design via the Future of Workplace Charter.

- 2024 evaluation results (employees):
  - Residual E&S risks by workforce exposure: freedom of association/collective bargaining (6.01%), discrimination (0.68%), health & safety (5.46%), working conditions (0.54%).
  - Country focus areas:
    - Freedom of association/collective bargaining: China, Colombia, UAE, USA, Hong Kong, Hungary, India, Malaysia, Romania, Serbia, Turkey, Ukraine.
    - Discrimination: Burkina Faso, Côte d’Ivoire, Equatorial Guinea, Italy, Poland.
    - Health & safety: Burkina Faso, Côte d’Ivoire, Romania, Togo.
    - Working conditions (ILO standards): Burkina Faso, Côte d’Ivoire, Equatorial Guinea, Hungary.

- Suppliers and subcontractors:
  - Quarterly tracking of E&S indicators on suppliers and tenders.
  - Coverage and criteria:
    - 100% of high/medium-high risk sourcing categories have formal E&S requirements for tenders; ~100 categories covered overall.
    - 98.6% of tenders in high E&S risk categories included E&S criteria in 2024.
  - Capability and oversight:
    - Tool developed for controversies linked to forced labour.
    - 100% of active buyers trained in Sustainable Sourcing; 98.5% completed Climate Fresk training.

- E&S risk management in business activities:

- Outlook and planned developments (2025):

  - Employees: EUR 100m to reduce gender pay gap; target 35% women in senior leadership by 2026; extend remote working charter; global social benefits via UNI agreement; strengthen engagement and wellbeing; promote Culture of Dialogue; continue social dialogue and listening channels; deploy “Care for You” wellbeing provisions; monthly psychosocial risk indicators and additional indicators during transformations; foster new DE&I employee collectives and disseminate recommendations.
  - Suppliers: progressively require minimum 15% E&S weighting in tenders for high-risk categories in the international market by 2025; extend E&S risk management to newly integrated sourcing entities.

- Overall theme: Continuous improvement of duty of care via structured governance, data-driven monitoring, stakeholder engagement, targeted country actions, supplier oversight, employee wellbeing initiatives, and alignment with regulatory standards (CSRD).

structure.title: Societe Generale group’s sustainability statement in a nutshell
structure.heading: Societe Generale group’s sustainability statement in a nutshell
structure.start_phrase: For the first time in 2024, Societe Generale goup publishes a sustainability statement as required by the European CSRD (Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive), transposed into French law.
structure.summary:
- Purpose and regulatory context: First-time publication of Societe Generale’s sustainability statement under the EU CSRD and ESRS, transposed into French law; limited assurance by external auditors per French H2A guidance; aim to harmonize ESG reporting and improve data quality.
- CSR strategy and governance: Group’s purpose guides a CSR strategy with four pillars—environmental transition, positive local impact, responsible employer, and culture of responsibility—overseen by the Executive Committee and Board, supported by a non‑voting director with environmental transition expertise.
- Double materiality: Material information determined via a double materiality assessment (impact and financial), leveraging existing risk and internal control frameworks; commitment to enhance methodologies as counterparties’ ESG data become more available.
- Climate change: A transition plan with decarbonization targets for corporate financing and life‑insurance savings portfolios, aiming for Paris Agreement alignment using sector‑specific methodologies; extensive employee training on sustainability; comprehensive E&S framework and sector policies; recognition of climate‑related risks and business opportunities.
- Own workforce: Approximately 119,000 employees in 60+ countries; “Responsible Employer” policies covering DEI and anti‑discrimination, occupational health, freedom of association and global agreement with UNI Global Union, attractive compensation, and continuous skills development; support for employee volunteering.
- Consumers and end users: Client‑centric Code of Conduct; policies on access to banking, responsible marketing, and protection of personal and confidential data.
